doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

title: First encountering Bob Wilber and Sidney Bechet
summary: At fifteen she saw a Melody Maker article about Bechet's young student Bob Wilber; she later knew him as a friend and thought of jazz as in Really the Blues.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Were you aware of Bob Wilber’s music before you met?

Oh yes. I can remember being in my grandmother’s kitchen. My grandmother lived in a working class type of cottage, and she had one small mirror, and it was sort of what men use for shaving you know, they would shave over the kitchen sink you see like this. And I remember putting on this green head scarf, it was very popular in those days to wear a head scarf and you sort of made it look very sheik and so on, and I can remember looking at myself in the mirror and then my eye catching an article from the Melody Maker, which was the — mostly jazz in those days, it’s not anymore sadly — and there was an article and it said Sidney Bechet takes on a young student from Scarsdale. And I thought to myself that’s who I want. And I was fifteen.

No. I was 15 years old, and I can remember looking at myself in the mirror and thinking, oh yes, you look kind of cute you know in this thing, and looking at this photograph, that’s what I want. That’s the first time. And I said I’m not being contrary, but when I said I didn’t plan my life, that’s when I said something that I wanted. And I wrote to Bob. I wrote to the Commodore Music Shop and said, “I know you know everybody, could you get me some autographs and photographs?” And Bob apparently said he didn’t get the letter but whether he did or not he subsequently said that he did. But I was fascinated by him, always fascinated by him, always. And although we had a number of meeting, he would come to our summer house in Saratoga when I was married to my former husband, and we would see each other as friends with no thought at all of any escapade, we just loved to talk about jazz. It was like a dream come true to be with somebody that you felt you already knew so well, and I admired him. I admired this young man who could have gone any route, and he denied his parents their ambition for him, to go off and be a jazz musician you know. I didn’t realize that jazz musicians had three or four square meals a day and slept in lovely beds with nice clean sheets and everything. I thought it was all like really the blues. I mean when I read Really the Blues, I read it surreptitiously, like you’d read Henry Miller you know? I was sort of hoping that no one was going to see what you were reading. I mean I thought it was that naughty.
Sometimes it is, but not always.
No but I was thinking that it was always, that all jazz musicians were the way that they were portrayed by Mezz Mezzrow. And it’s not so.
